# Volume 1 — CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“NURSE, you have to play Elaine, Nell,” Isolde stated. “It would be impossible for me to find the bravery needed to drift down to that spot.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0000 }

“Neither do I,” Opal Pettigrew stated, shivering. “Floating downward does not bother me when two or three of us are occupying the flat and we are able to sit upright. During those times, it is enjoyable. However, lying flat and acting as if I were deceased—that is something I simply could not do. Fear would actually kill me.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0001 }

“Naturally, it would have a romantic quality,” Odette Pullen admitted, “yet I am certain I would be unable to remain motionless. Every minute or two, I would be sitting up to check my position and ensure I was not floating away too much. And Nell, you are aware that such actions would ruin the impression.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0002 }

“Yet having an Elaine with red hair is simply absurd,” Nell lamented. “Floating down holds no fear for me, and I would be thrilled to portray Elaine. Even so, it remains absurd. Because she possesses such light skin and such beautiful, long yellow hair, Opal should play Elaine—after all, Elaine had ‘all her bright hair streaming down,’ as you are aware. Furthermore, Elaine was known as the lily maid. And a red-headed individual is incapable of being a lily maid.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0003 }

“You have a complexion that is every bit as fair as Opal’s,” Isolde said fervently, “and since you sheared your hair, it has become far darker than it ever was.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0004 }

“Oh, do you truly believe that?” cried Nell, her face reddening delicately in her joy. “At times I have considered that possibility myself—yet I was too afraid to inquire of anybody, dreading they might say otherwise. Would you say it qualifies as auburn at present, Isolde?”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0005 }

“Yes, and to me it appears truly lovely,” Isolde remarked, gazing with admiration at the brief, soft ringlets that gathered across Nell’s head, secured by a most stylish black velvet ribbon and bow.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0006 }

At the edge of the pond, beneath Pear Hill, where a birch-fringed spit of land extended from the shore, they stood together; positioned at its end was a tiny wooden pier jutting into the lake to serve the needs of anglers and wildfowlers. Isolde was host to Opal and Odette on this midsummer afternoon, and Nell had joined the group to take part in their games.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0007 }

The majority of their leisure hours during that season had been passed by Nell and Isolde around and upon the water. Larkrise existed no longer, since Mr. Bell had unmercifully felled the small grove of trees located in his rear field during the spring. Nell, while not entirely oblivious to the poetic tragedy of the moment, had cried as she perched amid the remaining wood; nevertheless, her grief was quickly relieved, because, as she and Isolde remarked, mature girls who were thirteen, nearing fourteen, had outgrown such juvenile pastimes as playhouses, whereas the pond offered far more captivating activities. Angling for trout from the bridge proved magnificent, and the pair of girls taught themselves how to navigate the small, flat-bottomed dory that Mr. Pembroke maintained for hunting ducks.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0008 }

Nell proposed that Elaine be dramatized by them. Tennyson’s poem had been studied by them at school during the previous winter, because the English curriculum for the St. Brendan’s Island schools, set by the Superintendent of Education, required it. It had been analyzed, parsed, and generally shredded to fragments by them until the fact that any significance whatsoever remained for them was astonishing, yet the fair lily maid, Lancelot, Guinevere, and King Arthur had, nevertheless, turned into extremely vivid figures to them, and a hidden sorrow consumed Nell that Camelot had not been her birthplace. Those times, she remarked, “were so much more romantic than the present.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0009 }

An enthusiastic reception greeted Nell’s plan. Having found that launching the flat from the landing place caused it to float downstream beneath the bridge and eventually come ashore on a different, lower headland projecting at a bend in the pond, the girls recognized this. Having frequently descended in this manner, they found nothing that could be better suited for playing Elaine.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0010 }

“All right, Elaine will be my part,” Nell stated, giving in with hesitation, because despite her eagerness to enact the main role, her creative judgment required suitability for the role, a quality she believed her boundaries prevented her from possessing. “Opal, the role of King Arthur falls to you, Guinevere will be played by Odette, while Isolde has to take the part of Lancelot. However, the roles of the father and the brothers must be filled by you first. Due to space constraints preventing a pair of us from being in the flat simultaneously while one is reclined, the ancient mute manservant has to be omitted. Over its entire distance, the barge needs to be draped in the darkest samite by us. Isolde, that former black shawl belonging to your mother is going to work perfectly.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0011 }

Upon obtaining the dark wrap, Nell unfolded it across the level surface and subsequently stretched out along the base, shutting her eyes and crossing her hands across her chest.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0012 }

“Oh, she appears truly deceased,” murmured Opal Pettigrew anxiously, gazing at the motionless, pale small face beneath the swaying shadows cast by the birches. “It fills me with fear, girls. Is it really proper for us to perform in this manner, do you think? Mrs. Sowerby claims that any drama-acting is dreadfully sinful.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0013 }

“Opal, speaking of Mrs. Sowerby is something you ought not to do,” Nell said sternly. “It ruins the impression, given that these events take place centuries prior to the birth of Mrs. Sowerby. Odette, take charge of this. Elaine speaking after she has died makes no sense.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0014 }

Odette proved equal to the situation. A coverlet made of gold cloth did not exist, yet a yellow Japanese crepe vintage piano scarf served as a superb replacement. Getting a white lily was impossible at that moment, although putting a tall blue iris into a folded hand belonging to Nell produced a result that left nothing to be wished for.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0015 }

“Now, she’s completely prepared,” Odette said. “Her tranquil forehead needs our kisses, and, Isolde, your line is, ‘Sister, farewell forever,’ while yours, Opal, is, ‘Farewell, sweet sister,’ with both of you speaking in the most doleful tone you can manage. Nell, please try to smile just a bit. Remember that Elaine ‘lay as though she smiled.’ Much better. Now shove the flat away from shore.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0016 }

Consequently, the flat was launched, grinding harshly against a sunken old stake as it went. Isolde and Odette and Opal merely paused until they saw it captured by the flow and pointing toward the bridge, whereupon they scurried up through the trees, over the road, and down to the lower point of land where, in the roles of Lancelot and Guinevere and the King, they had to stand prepared to welcome the lily maid.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0017 }

As she drifted gently downward for several minutes, Nell thoroughly savored the romantic nature of her circumstances. Shortly thereafter, an event occurred that was entirely unromantic. Water started entering the flat. Within a brief span of time, Elaine had to hurry to her feet, gather her cloth of gold coverlet along with her dark samite pall, and stare helplessly at a large fissure in the floor of her barge where water was rapidly streaming in. The flat had lost the strip of batting nailed to it because of that pointed stake back at the landing. Although Nell was unaware of this cause, she quickly comprehended the perilous state she was in. Should this speed continue, the flat was bound to flood and go under well before drifting down to the lower headland. As for the oars, they had been left behind at the landing!
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0018 }

Nell uttered a tiny, choked shriek that went entirely unheard by anyone; although her face paled to the very edges of her mouth, she managed to maintain her composure. A single possibility remained—only one.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0019 }

“Terror overwhelmed me,” she recounted to Mrs. Wace on the following day, “and the duration felt like an eternity as the flat drifted toward the bridge while water continuously surged inside. Deeply devout prayers were offered by me, Mrs. Wace, yet my eyes remained wide open throughout, since it was clear that my only salvation from God depended on the flat drifting sufficiently near a bridge pile so I could ascend it. As you are aware, those supports are merely ancient logs possessing numerous knots along with protruding broken limbs. Praying was appropriate, yet keeping a vigilant lookout constituted my own responsibility, a fact of which I was keenly aware. Repeating continually, I simply uttered, ‘Lord, guide the flat next to a post and the remaining effort will be mine.’ A person hardly considers composing elaborate entreaties during such a crisis. Nevertheless, my plea received a response, because the flat collided directly against a log briefly, allowing me to sling both the scarf and the shawl across my shoulder and haul myself onto a large, fortunate projection. Thus I remained, Mrs. Wace, gripping that slick, ancient log without any means to ascend higher or descend. My situation lacked all romantic appeal, though such thoughts never crossed my mind then. Romance is far from one's mind when an icy death in the water has barely been avoided. An immediate prayer of thanks was offered by me, after which my complete focus shifted to maintaining a firm grip, because I realized returning to solid ground would likely require help from fellow humans.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0020 }

The bridge was passed by the flat, which then immediately went down in the middle of the river. Having been waiting for it on the lower headland, Opal, Odette, and Isolde witnessed its disappearance right in front of them and felt certain that Nell was submerged alongside it. Standing motionless for a brief instance, pale as sheets and petrified by the horrific event, they then began to run wildly up through the forest while screaming as loudly as possible, not even stopping to look toward the bridge when they traversed the main road. Their speeding bodies were spotted and their screams were heard by Nell, who was holding on for dear life to her unstable perch. Assisting hands would arrive before long, yet her situation was presently most unpleasant.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0021 }

Time ticked away, with every minute feeling like an hour to the wretched lily maid. What was keeping everyone? What had happened to the girls? What if every single one of them had fainted! What if no one ever arrived! What if exhaustion and cramps forced her to lose her grip! Gazing down at the sinister, green depths beneath her, which flickered with lengthened, greasy shadows, Nell shuddered. Her mind started proposing every kind of horrifying outcome to her.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0022 }

Subsequently, right when she believed she truly lacked the strength to bear the pain in her wrists and arms for one more second, Hugh Carrow rowed beneath the bridge aboard Gorham Pullen’s dory!
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0023 }

Hugh looked upward and, greatly to his surprise, saw a small white disdainful face gazing down at him with large, terrified yet also disdainful gray eyes.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0024 }

“Nell Harcourt! By what possible means did you end up in that place?” he blurted out.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0025 }

Before any response could be given, he hauled near the piling and reached out a hand. Nothing could prevent it; holding fast to Hugh Carrow’s hand, Nell clambered into the dory, sitting soaked and enraged in the stern while holding a soaking shawl and soggy crepe in her arms. Maintaining dignity under those conditions was undoubtedly a great challenge!
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0026 }

“What is the matter, Nell?” inquired Hugh, picking up his oars.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0027 }

“Elaine was the role we were acting,” Nell clarified icily, refusing to glance toward the man who saved her, “and it was required that I float to Camelot aboard the barge—or rather, the flat. Water started leaking into the flat, causing me to scale the pile. Help was being sought by the girls. Would you please be good enough to take me by boat to the landing?”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0028 }

Hugh helpfully oared toward the dock, whereupon Nell, refusing any help, leaped cleverly onto the land.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0029 }

“I am deeply grateful to you,” she stated in a disdainful manner while turning around. However, Hugh had likewise leapt out of the craft and at that moment placed a restraining hand upon her arm.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0030 }

“Nell,” he urged in a rush, “listen. Is it possible for us to be close friends? I am deeply regretful that I teased you about your hair back then. Vexing you was not my intention, as I simply intended it to be humorous. Furthermore, a great deal of time has passed. I genuinely believe your hair is remarkably attractive these days—truly I do. Let us become friends.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0031 }

Nell paused briefly. Beneath all her offended self-respect, she possessed a strange, newly born awareness that the expression, partly diffident and partly enthusiastic, in the hazel eyes of Hugh was a truly wonderful sight. A fast, unusual small throb occurred in her heart. However, the sharpness of her former resentment immediately reinforced her faltering resolve. The event from two years earlier returned to her memory with the same brightness as if it had happened the day before. Hugh had referred to her as “carrots” and had caused her humiliation in front of the entire school. Her anger, which to different and more mature individuals could appear as amusing as its origin, was apparently not at all lessened or tempered by the passage of time. She despised Hugh Carrow! She would not ever pardon him!
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0032 }

“No,” she stated with a chilly tone, “friendship between us will never happen, Hugh Carrow, nor is it something I desire!”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0033 }

“Very well!” Hugh leaped into his skiff, a flushed, furious hue rising in his cheeks. “I am never going to ask for your friendship again, Nell Harcourt. Nor do I even care!”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0034 }

With rapid, rebellious movements of his arms, he rowed off, while Nell ascended the sharp, fern-covered small trail beneath the maple trees. Even though her head was carried extremely high, a strange sensation of sorrow washed over her. It was nearly her desire to have given Hugh a different response. Naturally, his offense toward her had been awful, yet nevertheless—! Taking everything into account, Nell felt that sitting and weeping thoroughly might bring her some comfort. Because the aftermath of her panic and stiff hanging on was taking its toll, she was actually rather shaken.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0035 }

Midway along the track she encountered Odette and Isolde hurrying back toward the pond, bordering on an absolute panic. Nobody was present at Pear Hill, since both Mr. and Mrs. Pembroke were out. At that point Opal Pettigrew had surrendered to a fit of hysterics, where she was abandoned to pull herself together as she could, as Odette and Isolde sped across the Whispering Wood and over the stream to Grey Shutters. Upon arriving there, they discovered no one as well, because Thirza had traveled to Delford and Obed was baling hay in the rear field.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0036 }

“Oh, Nell,” Isolde gasped, virtually collapsing onto her neck while crying out of relief and joy, “oh, Nell—we believed—you had—drowned—and we considered ourselves murderers—since we had forced—you to—act as Elaine. And Opal has become hysterical—oh, Nell, in what way did you survive?”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0037 }

“I scrambled onto a pile,” Nell said tiredly, “and Hugh Carrow arrived in the dory belonging to Mr. Pullen and ferried me to the shore.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0038 }

“Oh, Nell, how magnificent of him! Why, it is incredibly romantic!” gasped Odette, finally gathering sufficient air to speak. “Naturally, you will talk to him following this.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0039 }

“Naturally I will not,” Nell retorted, briefly regaining her previous fire. “And Odette Pullen, I never wish to listen to the term ‘romantic’ anymore. Girls, I am terribly apologetic that you were so terrified. The responsibility is entirely mine. I am convinced that my birth occurred beneath an unfortunate star. Every action I take lands myself or my most cherished friends in trouble. Isolde, we have managed to lose your father’s flat, and I possess a foreboding that our permission to row upon the pond will be revoked.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0040 }

Nell’s foreboding turned out to be far more reliable than such feelings usually are. Deep panic swept through the families of Pembroke and Abernethy as the occurrences of that afternoon were disclosed.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0041 }

“Is there any chance you will gain some sense, Nell?” Thirza groaned.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0042 }

“Oh, yes, I think I will, Thirza,” Nell replied with optimism. Having given way to a good cry in the welcoming privacy of the east gable, she had calmed her nerves and recovered her usual bright mood. “I think my prospects of becoming sensible are brighter now than ever.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0043 }

“I fail to understand how,” Thirza remarked.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0044 }

“Well,” Nell clarified, “a fresh and useful lesson has been taught to me today. From the moment I arrived at Grey Shutters, errors have been made by me, and every single blunder has assisted in healing me of a major fault. Being involved with the amethyst brooch healed my habit of tampering with items that were not mine. My blunder in the Whispering Wood healed my tendency to let my imagination overpower me. My blunder with the liniment cake healed my culinary neglect. Altering my hair’s color healed my self-conceit. My hair and nose are never on my mind these days—or at least, only on rare occasions. And what I did wrong today will heal my excessive romanticism. The realization has come to me that attempting romance in Brierley serves no purpose. Achieving it was likely simple in camelot with its towers centuries in the past, yet current times do not value romance. Thirza, I am certain you will notice a significant positive change in my behavior regarding this very shortly.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0045 }

“I certainly trust that will be the case,” Thirza remarked with doubt.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0046 }

However, Obed, who had remained silent where he sat in his corner, placed a hand upon Nell’s shoulder after Thirza departed.
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0047 }

“Do not abandon every bit of your romance, Nell,” he murmured bashfully, “having some of it is beneficial—certainly not a great deal—yet retain a bit of it, Nell, retain a bit of it.”
{: #nw-v01-c28-p0048 }
